title: POC scoping - capacity & autoscale - Zenith Labs
summary: POC scoping focused on capacity sizing and autoscale strategy for a 3-week POC. Customer wants predictable p95 latency <= 250ms for gen workloads and safe burst handling. Recommended baseline reserved GPUs with burst to additional capacity, plus fallback to quantized model variants and hosted tier. Action items include running a baseline benchmark, sharing config/pricing, and scheduling lab run next week.
next_steps: Redwood: share preliminary pricing and reserved GPU config (John) by 2025-07-18
Zenith: provide sample production traces and token distribution (Sara) by 2025-07-17
Schedule benchmark window with Redwood lab (Maya + Raj) for week of 2025-07-21
Redwood: send security docs (SOC2, ISO) and KMS integration notes (John)
action_items: John Park - send preliminary pricing & reserved capacity proposal - Due: 2025-07-18
Sara Lopez - upload sample traces and typical prompt/token distributions to shared drive - Due: 2025-07-17
Maya Chen - set up benchmark test plan and tools (locust/jmeter scripts) - Due: 2025-07-20
Raj Patel - confirm network egress/VPC requirements for lab run - Due: 2025-07-20
transcript:
[00:00] John Park: Alright, good afternoon everyone thanks for joining, uh this is John from Redwood, with Maya our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:06] Amir Khan: Hi John, yeah doing well, Amir here. Thanks for setting this up.
[00:10] Sara Lopez: Sara on the call. Quick heads up I'm juggling another meeting so I might be a little delayed at times.
[00:15] Raj Patel: Raj here from infra. We wanted to focus on capacity and autoscale for the POC so we can size things right.
[00:21] Maya Chen: Great, that's the plan. Today we want to agree on success criteria, get a sense of your workload sizing, and propose a reserved GPU + burst strategy plus fallback options for the POC.
[00:33] Amir Khan: High level: we're evaluating Redwood to replace a mix of hosted API calls and an internal inference pool. For the POC we want to validate latency and cost tradeoffs. Success criteria are primarily p95 latency under 250ms for our gen model at typical load, plus acceptable cost per 1k requests.
[00:49] John Park: Makes sense. Can you walk us through current traffic shape? QPS, payload size, and peak characteristics?
[00:55] Sara Lopez: Sure - average qps is about 10 req/s during the day, peaks at 40 req/s for short bursts. Most requests are text-generation with avg tokens per request about 200 tokens, and we have a smaller embeddings pipeline ~5 req/s. Latency currently varies a lot, we see tail spikes during concurrency.
[01:13] Raj Patel: Also we need to ensure data residency and KMS integration for keys - we'll need a VPC/private deployment for the POC or at least dedicated.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Understood, we can run this as Redwood Dedicated POC with reserved GPUs in your VPC. For sizing, initial recommendation is 2 reserved A100-80GB equivalent GPUs to handle baseline steady-state, with autoscale/burst up to 6 GPUs for peaks. That gives headroom for your 40 req/s bursts with target p95.
[01:38] Amir Khan: Can you translate that into latency and tokens/sec? I want to be able to predict p95 given our 200-token average.
[01:43] Maya Chen: Rough order: a single A10080 instance with our optimized runtime on that model handles roughly 300 tokens/sec for the gen model (this is workload-dependent). So two GPUs -> ~600 tokens/sec. At 40 req/s * 200 tokens = 8k tokens/sec needed at peak, so sustained peaks require autoscale to additional GPUs. With 6 GPUs you'd have ~1.8k tokens/sec per GPU? Sorry, let me rephrase: 6 GPUs -> 6 * 300 = 1800 tokens/sec capacity which meets the burst for 8k tokens/sec? Hmm that's inconsistent, let me restate carefully: our internal rough numbers are 300 tokens/sec per GPU for that model; for 8k tokens/sec you would need ~27 GPUs which is obviously wrong, so we need to check units.
[02:20] John Park: (laughs) This is why synthetic numbers mislead. Let's anchor: 40 req/s * 200 tokens = 8,000 tokens per second total. If one GPU does 300 tokens/sec, you need ~27 GPUs for fully synchronous single-token stepping. But we rarely run fully synchronous; we use batching, prefix caching, and KV cache reuse to reduce effective token throughput. For interactive chat, KV cache helps a lot. For your typical dialog where prior context is cached, effective tokens/sec required is much lower. So the autoscale numbers depend heavily on cache hit rate and batching.
[02:50] Sara Lopez: Our workloads have a lot of repeated prefixes (similar system prompts) so we expect good cache hits. We can provide traces.
[02:57] Raj Patel: So for the POC we don't need to provision 27 GPUs. What's realistic for a 3-week POC to validate tail latency?
[03:05] Maya Chen: Realistic approach: reserve 2 GPUs to cover steady-state with good caching and batching. For bursts, enable burst capacity that adds ephemeral GPUs (up to 6) to handle short spikes. If bursts exceed that, put fallback policies: (1) route overflow to a quantized 8-bit variant of the model (lower mem, slightly lower quality) hosted on cheaper nodes, and (2) as a last resort connect to a hosted tier with throttling and graceful degradation. That combination prevents failed requests while still measuring degradation.
[03:35] Amir Khan: What's the impact on latency when falling back to quantized variant? p95 goes up how much?
[03:40] Maya Chen: In our benchmarks a well-quantized INT8/4-bit variant increases generation latency by ~10-20% but often keeps p95 within acceptable range; quality drop is model-dependent. We'll include head-to-head comparison in the benchmark.
[03:52] Sara Lopez: For the quantized fallback, we care about stopped hallucinations and perf regressions. We'll run a set of prompts and metric suites.
[03:58] John Park: Good - include quality gauges: ROUGE/BLEU style for structured outputs, and human eval samples for open generation. Also instrument token/parsing errors.
[04:08] Raj Patel: Network wise any special egress or VPC peering needed for the burst GPUs if they're ephemeral? We're sensitive to egress costs and need to keep traffic in the VPC.
[04:16] Maya Chen: For Dedicated POC in a VPC we can keep burst GPUs inside your VPC boundary; we can provision ephemeral workers in the same network. There are a few constraints if you want air-gapped on-prem but for cloud VPC it's straightforward. We'll send a network checklist.
[04:28] Amir Khan: Timeline: we want the POC to run 3 weeks: week 0 prep/config, week 1 baseline runs, week 2 stress/peak runs, week 3 validation and final report. Is that feasible?
[04:38] John Park: Yes that's our typical cadence. We'll need your traces and a signed PO for reserved capacity or short-term commit. For the POC reserved we can do a month term or even a trial-reserved with credits.
[04:48] Sara Lopez: For success criteria let's be explicit: p95 latency <= 250ms on gen workloads for typical sessions with cache enabled, ability to handle 40 req/s bursts with no more than 2x cost increase, and quality delta <= 5% on our evaluation set when using quantized fallback.
[05:05] Maya Chen: I like those. We'll add reliability: error rate < 1% and no request failures during the benchmark window. We'll also capture cold-start behavior.
[05:13] John Park: For benchmarks we'll run three profiles: baseline (reserved only), burst profile (simulate sudden 2-3 min peaks at 40-60 req/s), and degradation path (saturate beyond burst to observe fallback). We'll measure p50/p95/p99, token/s, KV cache hit rate, and cost per 1k requests.
[05:28] Amir Khan: How do we simulate user distribution? We can replay traces.
[05:30] Maya Chen: Perfect — replay traces are best. If you can export a 24h slice we'll run it to get realistic batching and cache behavior.
[05:36] Raj Patel: For autoscaling rules what are recommended thresholds? CPU/GPU metrics or custom request queue depth?
[05:40] Maya Chen: We recommend multi-signal autoscaler: queue depth + GPU utilization + observed latency. For example, scale-out when avg GPU util > 70% for 30s or queue depth > X for 15s, and scale-in conservatively (e.g., util < 30% for 2m) to avoid flapping. Also include cooldowns and a burst pool separate from reserved capacity so reserved remains stable.
[06:00] Sara Lopez: What's the minimum scale step? Do we add single-GPU nodes or multi-GPU nodes?
[06:04] Maya Chen: The POC cluster will use single-GPU workers to give fine-grained autoscale steps. For production you can choose multi-GPU packs if you prefer lower overhead. We'll provision ephemeral single-GPU workers for burst.
[06:14] Amir Khan: Costs: how does reserved vs burst pricing work for POC?
[06:17] John Park: For reserved capacity you pay a fixed hourly reserved rate (we'll send numbers). Burst is billed at a higher per-hour on ephemeral nodes. For short bursts the effective cost is modest. We'll provide an estimated cost model in the proposal.
[06:28] Raj Patel: Fallback routing: can the system automatically route to a different model variant by policy? For example, if response latency > 300ms for more than 10% of requests route new requests to quantized variant.
[06:37] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood supports policy-based routing: route rules based on latency, capacity, region, and per-customer quotas. You can define canary rules and automatic fallback thresholds. We'll include a sample policy.
[06:47] Amir Khan: Observability: we need token-level cost, per-route latency, and tracing to tie back to user sessions for debugging.
[06:54] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdown, per-model/per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks you can emit to your monitoring. We'll instrument the benchmark to push traces into your Datadog/Prometheus.
[07:05] Sara Lopez: For the quality evaluation we'll need a baseline from our current infra to compare. We'll provide the same evaluation prompts.
[07:10] John Park: Great. So deliverables: benchmark run + report with p50/p95/p99, cost estimates, KV cache hit rate, autoscale events timeline, and recommendation for reserved size and burst cap.
[07:20] Raj Patel: On security docs: can you confirm SSO, RBAC, and KMS flow? We need SAML and ability to rotate keys.
[07:27] John Park: Yes we'll attach SOC2 and KMS integration docs; SAML SSO and RBAC are supported.
[07:32] Amir Khan: Any risks you see for this POC?
[07:34] Maya Chen: Biggest risk is mismatch in token throughput assumptions — if cache hit rate is lower than expected you may need more GPUs or higher burst caps. Also model quantization can degrade quality; we'll quantify that. We'll mitigate by running early baseline and a short warm-up period to populate caches.
[07:49] Sara Lopez: Sounds good. For benchmarks, can we also test cold-start latencies for new sessions? We sometimes see huge cold starts.
[07:56] Maya Chen: Absolutely, we'll include cold-start scenarios and measure first-token latency and end-to-end.
[08:02] John Park: Alright let's recap and assign owners. John will send pricing and reserved config; Maya will own benchmark plan and scripts; Sara will provide traces; Raj will validate VPC/network checklist; Amir will sign off on POC timeline pending pricing.
[08:18] Amir Khan: That's right. Aim to have the benchmark window the week of July 21st.
[08:22] John Park: We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark window and a short pre-benchmark readiness call.
[08:28] Sara Lopez: Quick question — when you say quantized fallback, is that an automated model swap or do we need to maintain two model endpoints?
[08:33] Maya Chen: It's an automated swap by policy but under the hood it's two endpoints (the main and the quantized variant). Redwood routes traffic per policy and can do gradual ramp or full switch.
[08:42] Raj Patel: Ok thanks everyone.
[08:44] John Park: Thanks all; we'll send the docs and follow-ups.
[08:48] Amir Khan: Thanks, bye.
[08:50] [call ends]
